title: Snap, Not Slide
description: Reid's broken fence, a 1,300 km rupture in 8 minutes, and why foreshocks are only known in hindsight

concepts.title: Elastic Rebound
concepts.contentHtml:
Just after 5:12 in the morning on April 18, 1906, the San Andreas fault slipped beneath northern California. Violent shocks punctuated strong shaking that lasted some 45 to 60 seconds.1 When it stopped, a fence near Bolinas in Marin County that crossed the fault had been cut in two, its halves offset by about 8.5 feet (2.6 meters).2 Elsewhere the jump was bigger: resurveys of the ground put the slip at up to 7.5 meters at Tomales Bay and 8.6 meters at Shelter Cove.3

Henry Fielding Reid, a geology professor at Johns Hopkins University, set out to explain those offsets. Surveys repeated after the quake showed that the ground had moved most right beside the fault, and less and less with distance from it, so a line that had been straight across the fault was now curved.4 Reid concluded that the earthquake was an elastic rebound: the crust had slowly stored elastic strain, then released it all at once.5

A rubber band shows the idea. Stretch it slowly and it stores energy; cut it and the energy comes out in an instant. Now picture a fence built straight across the fault. As the Pacific plate moves northwest, the fence is slowly dragged into an S shape. When the fault slips, the bend springs back and both halves are straight again, but now they are offset.6

Reid's idea turned the old order around: the faulting causes the earthquake, not the other way round.7 It also explains the timetable. On USGS estimates, 1906-sized earthquakes on this part of the San Andreas come about every 200 years,8 so strain that builds for two centuries is spent in under a minute.

concepts.title: How a Rupture Runs
concepts.contentHtml:
On December 26, 2004, a fault beneath the sea off Sumatra began to break, and it kept breaking for minutes. Using Japan's Hi-Net seismic array as a giant antenna, seismologists tracked the rupture as it ran north: about 1,300 kilometers in roughly 8 minutes, at about 2.8 kilometers per second.1 In both duration and extent, it was the longest rupture ever recorded.2

An earthquake, in other words, is not a jolt at a single point. The rupture begins at one spot, the focus, and its leading edge, the rupture front, spreads along the fault like a lengthening crack in a car windshield, and as the two sides lurch past each other they send out the seismic waves that shake the ground.3 Ruptures vary enormously in length. The 1906 San Francisco rupture was 477 kilometers long; the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake broke about 40.4

Which way the two sides move depends on how the crust is being stressed, and geologists sort faults into three main groups:5

  • Normal faults form where the crust is pulled apart. The block above the sloping fault slides down it.
  • Reverse, or thrust, faults form where the crust is squeezed. The upper block is pushed up the slope.
  • Strike-slip faults can form under either kind of stress. The blocks slide horizontally past each other.

Spreading zones mostly have normal faults, subduction zones thrust faults, and transform faults strike-slip.6 The 1906 earthquake, which baffled geologists of the day with its large horizontal displacements,7 was strike-slip.

concepts.title: Foreshocks and Aftershocks
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2011 a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck Japan, and for two days it was the mainshock. Then the magnitude 9.1 earthquake and tsunami arrived, and the 7.3 became a foreshock.1 Nothing about an earthquake marks it as a foreshock when it happens. The label comes only in hindsight, if something bigger follows, and only a small fraction of earthquakes are followed by a larger one.2

Aftershocks are far more orderly. In 1894 the Japanese seismologist Fusakichi Omori formulated their law: after the main shock, the frequency of aftershocks decreases hyperbolically with time.3 Put simply, the rate is roughly inversely proportional to the time since the mainshock, so there are about 10 times as many aftershocks on the first day as on the tenth.4 A century on, studies were still finding that a modified form of Omori's formula describes aftershock decay well.5

The rate falls, but the sizes do not. Aftershock magnitudes don't shrink with time, so a large aftershock can still strike late in a sequence.6 A second rule of thumb, Båth's law, deals with size: on average the largest aftershock is about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than its mainshock, whatever the mainshock's size.7 After a magnitude 7.0, then, the biggest aftershock is typically around 5.8. Because that is only an average, USGS aftershock forecasts are given as probabilities, including the probability of a later, larger earthquake.8

title: Waves Through Rock
description: Three kinds of wave, Zhang Heng's dragon seismoscope, and warnings that outrun the shaking

concepts.title: P, S and Surface Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
A strong earthquake tends to arrive in stages. The first sign is often a sharp thud as the compressional waves hit, then come the shear waves, and last the rolling "ground roll" of the surface waves.1 Each is a different way for rock to carry energy, and each travels at its own speed.

P waves (primary, or compressional) are the fastest, at about 6 kilometers per second in surface rock.2 They squeeze and stretch the rock in the direction they travel, the way sound compresses and expands air, and they cross fluids such as water as well as solid rock.3 Some of the vibrations are high enough in frequency to be heard.4

S waves (secondary, or shear) shake the rock at right angles to their path, up and down or side to side. They are about 1.7 times slower than P waves and cannot cross liquids, which is how they gave away Earth's liquid outer core.5 Near the surface they move at about 3.4 kilometers per second.6

P and S waves are body waves, traveling through the Earth. Surface waves travel along its surface instead, and they usually carry the strongest vibrations and probably cause most of the damage done by earthquakes.7 There are two kinds. Love waves shake the ground entirely from side to side.8 Rayleigh waves roll it, up and down and forward and back, and most of the shaking people feel in an earthquake comes from them.9

concepts.title: Finding the Epicenter
concepts.contentHtml:
In about 132 CE the Chinese astronomer and mathematician Zhang Heng described an instrument for sensing earthquakes, the earliest seismoscope known.1 It was a large bronze vessel, perhaps 2 meters across, with eight dragons around the top and a frog beneath each one. When the ground shook, a ball dropped from one dragon's mouth into the open mouth below.2 The original is lost; only its description survived, and modern scholars have tried to rebuild it from that.3

Its fame rests on a story in the Houhan Shu, the Book of the Later Han. One day a ball fell, but nobody at court had felt anything, and the device was taken for a failure. Days later a messenger arrived from a town about 400 miles (640 km) away with news of an earthquake.4 That Longxi earthquake is the only one the seismoscope is known to have detected.5 Working from the Houhan Shu's description, a 2006 study dates it to December 13, 134 CE, rather than the often-cited 138, and puts it at about magnitude 7.6

Seismologists now locate a quake with a clock. P and S waves leave the focus together, but the S waves fall behind, so the gap between their arrivals grows with distance, like the gap between lightning and thunder. Multiply the S-minus-P time in seconds by 8 and you get a very rough distance in kilometers.7 (The 8 comes from the speeds: at about 6 and 3.4 kilometers per second, the S wave loses roughly one second on every 8 kilometers.) In one worked example, P and S arrive 24 seconds apart, and travel-time curves put the quake 215 kilometers away.8

One station gives only a distance: a circle on the map, with the epicenter somewhere on its edge. Circles drawn around three stations meet at a single point, the epicenter, a method called trilateration.9

concepts.title: Seconds of Warning
concepts.contentHtml:
On October 1, 2007, the Japan Meteorological Agency began sending Earthquake Early Warnings to the public through TV, radio and other media.1 The warning predicts nothing. It wins a race. Seismic waves travel through the shallow Earth at 0.5 to 3 miles (roughly 1 to 5 kilometers) per second, while an alert crosses communication networks almost instantly.2

It also exploits the head start of the P wave. Sensors near the epicenter pick up the fast but weak P waves, the alert goes out, and people and machines get seconds to act before the slower, stronger S and surface waves arrive.3 The farther you are from the epicenter, the more warning you get.4

The US West Coast followed with the USGS's ShakeAlert system. Statewide public alerts began in California in October 2019, then expanded to Oregon in March 2021 and Washington in May 2021.5 What do a few seconds buy? Trains can be slowed and elevators controlled before the shaking starts.6 Surgeons and dentists can stop delicate procedures.7

The catch is the blind zone, the region around the epicenter where no warning is possible because the strong shaking has already arrived by the time the alert is generated. Better networks can shrink it.8 Detecting a quake and sending the alert both take time, so there will always be a late-alert zone near the epicenter.9 And even outside it, JMA warns, the gap between alert and strong tremors is a matter of seconds, between several seconds and a few tens of seconds.10

title: How Big Was It?
description: Richter's yardstick, shaking in Roman numerals, and the giants that sped up Earth's spin

concepts.title: Size Versus Shaking
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1994 Northridge earthquake in Los Angeles had one magnitude, 6.7, but the shaking it caused had many values: intensity IX (violent) near the epicenter, V (moderate) about 60 to 200 miles away, and I (not felt) farther out.1 How big a quake is and how hard it shakes a place are different questions, so seismologists keep two kinds of scale.

Magnitude measures the quake itself. The first magnitude scale was devised in 1935 by the American seismologists Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg.2 The name was Harry Wood's suggestion, chosen to keep the new instrumental scale apart from the intensity scales already in use.3 It worked only for California quakes within 600 km of one kind of instrument, the Wood-Anderson torsion seismograph.4 Zero did not mean no earthquake. It sat near the smallest shocks the seismographs of the 1930s could detect, and today's more sensitive instruments record quakes with negative magnitudes.5

Intensity describes what the shaking did at one spot, from people waking up to furniture moving to damaged chimneys. The scale used in the United States, the Modified Mercalli, was drawn up in 1931 by the same Harry Wood, with Frank Neumann. It runs in Roman numerals from imperceptible shaking to catastrophic destruction, and it has no mathematical basis: it is a ranking of observed effects.6

Today the public does much of the observing. The USGS Did You Feel It? survey groups the answers people send in by ZIP code or city and gives each place a single intensity.7 Even a reply of "not felt" counts, because it helps mark the edge of the area where the quake was felt.8

concepts.title: Measuring the Break Itself
concepts.contentHtml:
About three minutes after the Tōhoku earthquake struck on March 11, 2011, the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its first tsunami warning, based on a quick magnitude of 7.9.1 That fast method saturates for quakes much larger than magnitude 8. The agency raised its figure to 8.4 at 4 pm, computed a moment magnitude of 8.8 at 5:30 pm, and on March 13 revised it to 9.0.2

Saturation is why the older scales fail on giants. They read the height of one kind of seismic wave, and once a rupture grows longer than those waves (usually 5 to 50 km), a bigger break no longer makes a proportionally bigger wave, as Hiroo Kanamori showed in 1977.3 On the Richter scale, no earthquake has ever registered above 8.6: that was the 1960 Chile earthquake, whose moment magnitude is 9.5.4

The cure was to measure the break itself. Seismic moment is rigidity × area × slip: how strong the rock along the fault is, how much fault surface slipped, and how far it moved.5 In 1979 Tom Hanks and Kanamori turned moment into the moment magnitude scale, Mw, built to agree with the older scales where they work and to keep counting where they stop.6

Because moment grows with fault area, the size of a fault caps the size of its quakes. If the whole San Andreas Fault, about 1,400 km long, slipped 10 m at once, USGS calculates it would make a magnitude 8.47; the South American subduction zone, about 6,400 km long and slipping 40 m, would make a 9.86.7 A magnitude 10 would need a fault about 14,000 km long, over a third of the way around the planet, slipping 30 m.8

concepts.title: The Record Holders
concepts.contentHtml:
The top of the list belongs to the Valdivia earthquake in southern Chile: magnitude 9.5, on May 22, 1960.1 Next comes the Great Alaska earthquake of March 27, 1964, magnitude 9.2: the largest in US history and the second largest ever recorded with modern instruments. It swayed Seattle's Space Needle more than 1,200 miles away and sloshed waterways as far as the coasts of Texas and Louisiana.2 It was so large that it set the whole Earth ringing like a bell.3 The Sumatra earthquake of December 26, 2004 stands at 9.1,4 and so does Japan's Tōhoku earthquake of March 11, 2011.5 (Japan's own agency settled on 9.0.)

Quakes this big reshape the land. The Tōhoku fault slipped as much as 50 to 60 m over an area about 400 km long and 150 km wide.6 Japan's coast lurched east: on the Oshika Peninsula the ground moved more than 5.3 m, the largest shift Japan's national GPS network had ever detected.7

They even change how fast the planet turns. By shifting Earth's mass, Tōhoku should have made Earth spin a little faster, shortening each day by about 1.8 microseconds, by the calculation of Richard Gross at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.8 His estimate for Sumatra's 2004 quake was 6.8 microseconds: the effect depends on where a quake strikes and how its fault slips, not just on magnitude.9 Nobody will feel it: over a year, the length of the day rises and falls by about a millisecond, some 550 times the change from the earthquake.10

title: Where the Earth Breaks
description: The Ring of Fire, New Madrid far from any plate edge, and quakes set off by wastewater and gas

concepts.title: Around the Ring of Fire
concepts.contentHtml:
Trace the rim of the Pacific Ocean, from Chile up to Alaska and down past Japan, and you have outlined the world's greatest earthquake belt. About 81 percent of the planet's largest earthquakes strike along this circum-Pacific belt, nicknamed the Ring of Fire, where plates of mostly ocean crust are sinking, or subducting, beneath their neighbors.1 The second belt, the Alpide, runs from Java and Sumatra through the Himalayas and the Mediterranean into the Atlantic and accounts for about 17 percent, including the magnitude 9.1 off Sumatra in 2004.2 Subduction zones bring deep-ocean trenches, earthquakes from shallow to deep, and mountain ranges with active volcanoes, which supply the fire in the name.3

The giants come from one kind of fault. Where a plate dives, its top grinds beneath the plate above along a vast thrust fault called a megathrust. Off Japan the Pacific plate moves west at about 83 mm a year and starts its descent at the Japan Trench, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake was thrust faulting on that plate boundary.4 Before it, the largest quakes since 1900 were Kamchatka in 1952 (9.0), Chile in 1960 (9.5), Alaska in 1964 (9.2) and Sumatra in 2004, and all of them were megathrust events, where one plate subducts beneath another.5

Megathrusts win because moment grows with fault area, and few faults are so big. A subduction boundary can run for thousands of kilometers, and the 2004 Sumatra rupture was about 150 km wide, with slip of more than 20 m on the fault.6 Even the whole San Andreas Fault, breaking end to end, would fall short of magnitude 9.

concepts.title: Shocks in the Middle of a Plate
concepts.contentHtml:
In the winter of 1811–12 the Mississippi valley, deep inside North America, was hit by earthquakes whose area of strong shaking was two to three times that of the 1964 Alaska earthquake and ten times that of San Francisco's in 1906.1 There were three principal earthquakes, on December 16, 1811, January 23, 1812 and February 7, 1812.2 No seismographs existed, so sizes come from old accounts: studies range from 6.8 to 8.1 for the first quake, and the USGS hazard maps adopt 7.5.3

Accounts tell of the Mississippi running backward, for a few minutes in most versions.4 The USGS catalog gives the sober reading: local uplifts of the ground and waves moving upstream gave the illusion that the river was flowing upstream.5

On August 31, 1886, an earthquake wrecked Charleston, South Carolina, and killed 60 people. Hardly a building in the city escaped damage.6 Both struck inside the North American plate, far from its edges, and quakes like that are uncommon: fewer than 10 percent of all earthquakes occur within plate interiors. Old, weakened zones inside a continent can still fail under stresses that come from the plate's edges or the deeper crust.7

Eastern quakes also reach farther. East of the Rockies, an earthquake can be felt over an area as much as ten times larger than one of similar magnitude on the West Coast.8 When a magnitude 5.8 quake in Virginia rattled the East Coast in 2011, USGS geologist David Schwartz explained why: the eastern crust is older, colder and denser, so seismic waves travel much farther there.9

concepts.title: Earthquakes We Make
concepts.contentHtml:
By the Oklahoma Geological Survey's count, the state had about 2 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more a year before 2009. In 2014 it had 579, and in 2015, 903. Then the count fell: 624 in 2016, 304 in 2017 and 194 in 2018.1 The strongest, a magnitude 5.8 near Pawnee in September 2016, remains the largest earthquake ever located in Oklahoma.2

The main culprit was not fracking itself but wastewater. In the active areas, most of the fluid pumped into deep disposal wells was salty water that comes up with the oil, not water used to fracture the rock.3 Raising the fluid pressure deep underground weakens the clamping force that holds a fault shut, so a fault already close to failure can slip.4 In early 2016 the state's regulators called for a 40 percent cut in injection volume in the most active areas.5

Taking fluid out can do it too. Groningen, in the northeastern Netherlands, is the largest gas field in Europe, and its gas extraction has set off earthquakes since 1991.6 The strongest, magnitude 3.6 near Huizinge on August 16, 2012, was felt more strongly than anything before it.7 In 2024 Dutch leaders voted to halt all future production from the field because of the quakes.8

Mines, geothermal projects and reservoirs can trigger quakes as well. India's Koyna dam was filled in 1962, tremors soon followed, and on December 10, 1967, a magnitude 6.3 struck.9

title: Anatomy of a Tsunami
description: Why tsunami means harbor wave, jetliner speed at a meter high, and the sea that drains away first

concepts.title: What Moves the Water
concepts.contentHtml:
On 26 December 2004, along a fault off the coast of Sumatra, the floor of the Indian Ocean was pushed up by several meters.1 The sea above it had no choice but to rise too. That is what sets a tsunami apart from an ordinary wave. Wind ruffles only the surface, but a tsunami moves the entire water column, from the surface down to the seabed.2

Most tsunamis begin this way, at a subduction zone. For decades or centuries the edge of the overriding plate is dragged down and squeezed; in the earthquake it breaks free and springs seaward, lifting the seafloor and the water above it.3 The raised hump of water then slumps back under gravity, and as it seeks its old level the disturbance spreads outward in all directions as a set of very long waves. Earthquakes, or landslides set off by earthquakes, generated 88% of the tsunamis in NOAA's Global Historical Tsunami Database.4 But anything that suddenly shoves aside a large volume of water can do it: a landslide, a volcanic eruption, certain kinds of weather, or an asteroid or comet hitting the sea.5

The name records where people met them. Tsunami comes from the Japanese characters meaning "harbor wave."6 English speakers long called them tidal waves, but tides come from the pull of the Sun and Moon and have nothing to do with tsunamis, so the old name is simply wrong.7

concepts.title: Fast and Flat, Then Tall
concepts.contentHtml:
In the deep ocean a tsunami can move as fast as a jet plane, over 800 km/h, and cross an entire ocean in less than a day.1 The speed follows a simple rule: take the square root of gravity (9.8 meters per second squared) times the water depth. In 4,600 meters of water that comes to about 765 km/h, fast enough to get from Alaska's Aleutian Islands to Hawaii in about five hours.2 Depth sets the pace because the wave is moving the whole column of water, right down to the seabed.

Yet a ship in its path would hardly notice. Out at sea a tsunami is rarely more than about a meter high, and its crests can be hundreds of kilometers apart, so the surface lifts and sinks gently over many minutes. Sailors do not normally notice one passing beneath their hulls.3

Everything changes near land. As the water gets shallower, the tsunami slows down, its wavelength shortens, its height grows and its currents strengthen. By the shore most tsunamis have slowed to the speed of a car, about 30 to 50 km/h.4 (Try the rule on 10 meters of water: it gives about 36 km/h.) This growth in height as the wave climbs the continental shelf toward the coast is called shoaling.5 Even then a tsunami rarely curls over and breaks like a surf wave. Its wavelength is so long that it seldom gets steep enough to break.6 Instead it tends to rush ashore like a fast-rising flood, and keep on coming.

concepts.title: Drawback and the Wave Train
concepts.contentHtml:
In March 1964 a tsunami from the Good Friday earthquake in Alaska reached Crescent City, California, as a series of what were probably four waves. The first caused only minor flooding of shops near the shore.1 One family went back to their tavern to mop up and fetch the cash box. Rising water ripped the building off its foundation, and when their rescue boat capsized, everyone except the 27-year-old son drowned. Eleven people died in the town that night.2 The lighthouse keepers watched the fourth and largest wave arrive: first "the water withdrew as if someone had pulled the plug," draining three-quarters of a mile from the shore, and then a black wall of water came back.3

A tsunami is a series of waves, not a single one, often called the wave train.4 When a trough reaches the coast first, the sea suddenly drains away before the water rushes in, showing the seafloor, reefs and fish like a very low tide.5 This drawback is a warning, not a curiosity. Crests can arrive anywhere from about five minutes to two hours apart, and the first wave may not be the last, the largest or the most damaging. Big tsunamis often peak a couple of hours after they arrive and can go on for days.6

When scientists say how big a tsunami was, they often quote its run-up: the maximum height above sea level the water reaches on shore. Most run-ups are under about 3 meters (10 feet), but close to the source they can top 30 meters (100 feet).7 Run-up depends on the coast as much as the wave. Reefs, bays, river mouths and the slope of the beach all shape it, so a small, harmless tsunami in one place may be very large and violent a few miles away.8

title: The Biggest Waves
description: Lituya Bay's 524-meter run-up, the schoolgirl who cleared a beach, Tōhoku and Hunga Tonga

concepts.title: Lituya Bay, 1958
concepts.contentHtml:
On the evening of 9 July 1958, three fishing boats lay at anchor in Lituya Bay, a steep-walled, T-shaped inlet on the coast of southeast Alaska. At 10:16 pm a magnitude 7.8 earthquake ruptured the Fairweather fault, which runs right through the two arms at the head of the bay.1 The shaking sent about 40 million cubic yards (some 30 million cubic meters) of rock plunging into Gilbert Inlet from as high as 3,000 feet.2

The water had nowhere to go but up. It surged over the ridge on the far side of the inlet and washed out the forest to an altitude of 1,720 feet,3 about 524 meters, the highest run-up ever documented.4 A wave then swept down the whole bay toward the boats. Howard Ulrich, aboard the Edrie with his 7-year-old son, could not free his anchor, so he let out all his chain and steered into the wave. The boat shot up its face, the anchor chain snapped, and the Edrie rode over the crest still afloat.5 The Badger was thrown over the spit at the bay's mouth and wrecked, though its crew escaped in a skiff. The Sunmore vanished with the couple aboard.6

Lituya Bay was nothing like an ocean-crossing tsunami. A huge slide into a narrow, deep inlet throws up a local surge, the kind of event now often called a megatsunami. Near their source, landslide tsunamis can be larger than earthquake tsunamis and strike within minutes, but they usually lose energy quickly and rarely reach distant coasts.7

concepts.title: Indian Ocean, 2004
concepts.contentHtml:
On 26 December 2004, ten-year-old Tilly Smith was on Maikhao Beach in Phuket, Thailand, with her family. "I was on the beach and the water started to go funny," she said a few days later. "There were bubbles and the tide went out all of a sudden."1 Two weeks earlier her geography teacher, Andrew Kearney, had shown her class a video of a tsunami in Hawaii.2 She told her parents a tsunami was coming. Quick action by her mother and the hotel staff cleared the beach minutes before a huge wave crashed ashore, and it was one of the few beaches on Phuket where no one was killed.3

Most people around the Indian Ocean had no such warning. A magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra set off the deadliest tsunami in recorded history: UNESCO counts more than 227,000 dead across 15 countries and 1.6 million people displaced.4 There was no official tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean at the time, and NOAA puts part of the toll down to that gap and to how little people knew about tsunamis.5

Afterward the Indian Ocean nations decided to build their own warning system and asked UNESCO's Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission to coordinate it.6 On 12 October 2011, in a full-scale drill that replayed the 2004 earthquake, responsibility for advisories passed to new regional centers in Australia, India and Indonesia.7 Tilly's story became part of the case for teaching the warning signs too. Meeting her in 2005 as the UN's envoy for tsunami recovery, Bill Clinton called it "a simple reminder that education can make a difference between life and death."8

concepts.title: Tōhoku 2011 and Tonga 2022
concepts.contentHtml:
On 11 March 2011 the largest earthquake ever recorded in Japan, magnitude 9.1, struck off the country's east coast. It killed more than 18,000 people, most of them in the tsunami.1 Survey teams later traced the highest run-up to 38.9 meters in Iwate Prefecture,2 even though tide gauges along the coast recorded waves of 1 to 9 meters.3 Run-up can tower over the wave heights measured at the shore. Defenses built for smaller waves were overwhelmed. The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant was protected against tsunamis of at most 5.7 meters; the largest waves that hit it were estimated at over 14 meters, and the flooding knocked out every power source but one emergency generator, leading to a nuclear accident.4

Eleven years later a volcano, not an earthquake, sent tsunami waves around the world. When the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai exploded on 15 January 2022, tide gauges picked up tsunami waves not only across the Pacific but in the Atlantic and Indian oceans and the Caribbean and Mediterranean seas.5 The first waves arrived too early to have traveled through the water. They kept pace with a pressure wave in the air from the blast, racing outward at about 307 meters per second (some 1,100 km/h).6 A tsunami crossing the Pacific's average depth manages only about 198 meters per second, and the largest waves, which came later and stayed mostly in the Pacific, matched that slower pace.7 For those first waves, the volcano had pushed on the sea from above, through the air.

title: Memory in Mud and Stone
description: Japan's orphan tsunami of 1700, a village saved by a stone, and quakes counted in mud

concepts.title: The Orphan Tsunami of 1700
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1700, a tsunami came ashore in Japan. It drowned rice paddies and crops, washed away more than a dozen buildings and spread a fire that burned twenty more.1 Yet no earthquake had been felt. A village headman, with no shaking to warn him, wondered what to call the waves.2 For almost three centuries it was an orphan tsunami, a wave without a known parent.3

The parent was hiding across the Pacific, in the mud of the Washington coast. In 1987 Brian Atwater reported that tidal mud had buried lowlands there at least six times in 7,000 years, each time probably because the land suddenly dropped by half a meter to two meters.4 The eeriest clues are ghost forests: groves of weathered trunks standing dead in tidal marshes, killed when the ground sank and the tides moved in.5

In 1996 Kenji Satake and colleagues joined the two halves in the journal Nature. Records showed no large earthquake in 1700 in South America, Alaska or Kamchatka, which left Cascadia as the most likely source.6 From the Japanese accounts they put the quake at about 9 pm on 26 January 1700, with a magnitude near 9, big enough to rupture the whole length of the Cascadia subduction zone.7 Tree rings then tested the date. The drowned cedars had died between August 1699 and May 1700, a window that holds the date from Japan.8

concepts.title: Warnings from the Ancestors
concepts.contentHtml:
Beside the only road of Aneyoshi, a hamlet on Japan's northeast coast, a stone tablet gives an order: "Do not build your homes below this point!"1 In March 2011 the tsunami stopped about 300 feet (90 meters) below it, and the village beyond it was spared.2 It was no small wave. A university group reported that the tsunami reached its greatest height right there in Aneyoshi: 127.6 feet, nearly 39 meters, a record for Japan.3

The stone was paid for twice. According to the village leader, the 1896 tsunami left only two survivors; the village moved uphill, drifted back to the shore, and was struck again in 1933, leaving four. Only then did it move uphill for good, and the stone was placed.4 Hundreds of these tsunami stones dot Japan's coast, some more than six centuries old, but many towns rebuilt below them.5 "It takes about three generations for people to forget," one disaster researcher said.6

Off Sumatra, the island of Simeulue kept its memory in words. Nobody knows how many died in a tsunami there in 1907, but the island's legend tells of up to 70 percent of the people.7 Its word smong, "the ocean coming onto the land," stayed in the local language, and the stories carried the advice: after strong shaking, run to the hills.8 On 26 December 2004, waves at the north end of the island topped 10 meters less than 10 minutes after the shaking stopped. The islanders did not wait for a warning.9 Of the island's 78,128 people, local officials counted 7 killed by the tsunami.10

concepts.title: Reading Old Quakes
concepts.contentHtml:
In a 1978 study, geologist Kerry Sieh described trenches he had dug into marsh deposits on the San Andreas fault at Pallett Creek, about 55 kilometers northeast of Los Angeles. The layers held the marks of large quakes going back to the sixth century AD.1 Sharper radiocarbon dates later showed that the last 10 came in four clusters: a few decades apart within a cluster, with two to three centuries of quiet between them.2

This is paleoseismology. A quake that breaks the surface offsets the layers of sediment, and fresh sediment soon buries the break. Dating the layers below and above it, often by radiocarbon, brackets when the quake struck.3 On a sinking coast the clue is a sand sheet lying on a buried marsh soil. Its sand came from the sea, thins inland and holds the tiny shells of marine diatoms: the signature of a tsunami.4

Offshore, strong shaking sends sediment pouring down submarine canyons in underwater avalanches that settle as layers called turbidites. Off Washington, several canyons each hold 13 to 16 of them above the same marker, a layer of ash from Mount Mazama.5 That eruption, more than 7,600 years ago, formed Crater Lake in Oregon.6 If each canyon's flows had been set off separately, the channel below the point where they merge should hold 26 to 32. It holds 13: they were triggered together.7 In a 2012 USGS report, Chris Goldfinger's team traced this record back 10,000 years and counted 19 to 20 ruptures of all or nearly all of Cascadia, plus about two dozen smaller ones in the south.8 The youngest matches the quake of 1700, and in the north the great ones came on average every 500 to 530 years.9

title: Predict, Warn, Survive
description: Why nobody predicts quakes, Parkfield's late quake, the L'Aquila trial and what keeps people alive

concepts.title: Forecasts, Not Prophecies
concepts.contentHtml:
"Neither the USGS nor any other scientists have ever predicted a major earthquake." That is the US Geological Survey's own answer to whether quakes can be predicted.1 A true prediction has to name three things: the date and time, the location and the magnitude.2 Claims that leave one out, or are so vague that some quake will always fit, do not count.

What science can offer is a forecast: a probability over years or decades, like the chance of rain in a weather report. The 2014 Working Group on California Earthquake Probabilities put the chance of at least one magnitude 6.7 or larger quake striking the San Francisco Bay region before 2043 at 72 percent.3 A number like that shapes building codes and emergency plans, but it cannot tell anyone which year to worry.

Parkfield, a tiny town on the San Andreas fault, looked like the best chance to do better. Quakes of about magnitude 6 had struck there at fairly regular intervals, in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934 and 1966.4 The next was expected between 1988 and 1993.5 Scientists ringed the fault with instruments and waited. It came on 28 September 2004, more than a decade late, and became the best-recorded earthquake in the world up to that time.6 Even so, the instruments caught no obvious warning signs.7 In 1934 and 1966 a magnitude 5 foreshock had struck 17 minutes before the main shock; in 2004 there was none.8

concepts.title: When Warnings Go Wrong
concepts.contentHtml:
In the winter of 1975, officials in northeast China ordered the evacuation of Haicheng, a city of about a million people.1 For months there had been reports of shifting ground water and strange animal behavior, and then a swarm of small quakes, later recognized as foreshocks, set off the warning.2 The magnitude 7.3 quake struck on 4 February 1975 and killed 2,041 people. Without the evacuation, it was estimated, deaths and injuries would have topped 150,000.3

Haicheng could not be repeated. On 28 July 1976 a magnitude 7.6 quake hit the industrial city of Tangshan without warning: none of the signs seen near Haicheng appeared, and an estimated 250,000 people died.4

In 2009, after months of small tremors around the Italian city of L'Aquila, a senior civil protection official made reassuring statements that most experts say were false: he told reporters the stream of small tremors was discharging energy and made a big quake less likely.5 Days later a magnitude 6.3 quake killed 309 people.6 He and six scientists, all members of the national Major Risks Commission, were tried for falsely reassuring the public and failing to assess the risk properly, not, as is often said, for failing to predict the quake.7 A 2012 verdict found all seven guilty of manslaughter and sentenced each to six years in jail; in November 2014 an appeals court acquitted the six scientists.8 The official, Bernardo De Bernardinis, was cleared on 16 counts but convicted on 13, with his sentence cut to two years and suspended.9 As USGS seismologist Lucy Jones put it, "A technically correct prediction that is not used correctly is not a good prediction."10

concepts.title: Living with It
concepts.contentHtml:
When the magnitude 6.7 Northridge earthquake shook Los Angeles in 1994, USC University Hospital and its contents suffered no damage.1 The 8-story hospital stands on 149 base isolators that partly decouple it from the ground, and they cut the motion fed into the building by about two-thirds.2 Most buildings get their protection from strict building codes instead, which in quake-prone regions have greatly reduced the chance of collapse.3

Because few buildings collapse, the main danger indoors lies elsewhere. You are far more likely to be hurt by falling or flying objects, such as TVs, glass and bookcases, than to die in a collapsed building.4 So rescue teams and researchers teach Drop, Cover, and Hold On: drop before the earthquake drops you, take cover under a sturdy table or protect your head and neck with your arms, and hold on until the shaking ends.5

At the coast, the quake itself is the warning: the longer the shaking lasts, the more likely a tsunami is on its way.6 So is a sea that pulls back and bares the seafloor, or a roar from the ocean like a train or a jet. Do not wait for an official order: leave low ground and move to higher ground at once.7

For a tsunami from far away, with no shaking to feel, the warning comes from the deep. NOAA's DART stations pair a pressure recorder on the seafloor with a buoy at the surface, and the recorder can detect a tsunami just 1 centimeter high in 6,000 meters of water.8 Direct measurement also tackled false alarms: when DART was designed, about 75 percent of US tsunami warnings since the 1950s had been false.9
